Vignette: Mr. L. (Age 46, Software Engineer)

Mr. L. is a 46-year-old married man of South Eastern Asian descent who works as a senior software engineer. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly concerned about his irritability, social withdrawal, and a deepening sense of distance between them. He agrees that something is wrong, but struggles to articulate it beyond a vague sense of being "wired wrong" since returning from his deployment.

He tells his story quietly, often pausing to stare at a fixed point on the wall. The narrative begins in his late twenties. He was a promising programmer, but after the 2008 economic downturn, his job security felt precarious. Driven by a sense of duty and a desire for stable income for his future family, he joined the military as a reservist. He was deployed to a combat zone eleven years ago, serving as a communications specialist. He was not on the front lines, he explains, but his unit came under frequent indirect fire-mortars and rockets-at their forward operating base. He remembers the sound most clearly: a high-pitched whistle that would drop into a deafening thud, shaking the ground and the walls of his bunker. He says he "got used to it" at the time. He did his job, maintained the network, and came home.

He describes the first year back as a "gray fog." He returned to his software engineering role, but found the open-plan office unbearable. He would sit with his back to the wall, scanning the room for exits. The beep of a microwave or a dropped keyboard would make him jump, his heart hammering. He attributed it to "reverse culture shock" and assumed it would fade. It did not. He married his wife, a kind and patient woman, a few years later. They had two children. He tried to be present, but describes feeling like he was "watching his own life from behind a pane of glass."

In the present, his life has narrowed considerably. He works remotely, which he prefers, as it allows him to control his environment. His desk is positioned so he can see the front door and the windows. He keeps the television volume low, and flinches at the sound of a car backfiring or a helicopter passing overhead. He has not been to a movie theater or a crowded restaurant in over five years. He finds crowds "impossible"-he cannot focus on anything but the potential threat, his peripheral vision scanning for sudden movements.

His sleep is poor. He wakes multiple times a night, often with a start, convinced he heard the whistle of a mortar. He describes a recurring dream where he is back in his bunker, but the walls are made of drywall, and the ceiling is slowly collapsing. He does not talk about his deployment. When his wife asks, he becomes irritable and shuts down. He feels a deep, corrosive guilt, though he cannot pinpoint its source. He says he "should have been stronger," that others had it worse. He avoids news reports about the Middle East, and cannot watch movies with explosions or gunfire. He has stopped talking to his old Army friends. "They remind me of a person I don't want to be anymore," he says, his voice flat.

At work, he is functional but detached. He completes his coding tasks with mechanical precision, but has no interest in team meetings or collaborative projects. He feels his colleagues are "living in a different world," concerned with problems that seem trivial. He has been passed over for a promotion twice, which he says he does not care about, but his wife notes he was once ambitious and proud of his work.

He describes a constant, low-level sense of being on alert, as if a switch inside him is stuck in the "on" position. He feels disconnected from his children, unable to engage in their play. He loves them, he says, but the emotion feels distant, intellectualized. The worst part, he confides, is the feeling that he is a burden. He sees the worry in his wife's eyes and feels a deep shame. He came to therapy because he is tired of feeling like a ghost in his own life, but he is not sure if he can be reached. He sits forward in his chair, his hands clasped tightly, and waits.
